meta.title: Who really said "I must also have a dark side if I am to be whole"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Jung wrote a near-identical sentence in Collected Works vol. 16 — but the short line people share is trimmed and reordered, and Wikiquote lists it unsourced.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I must also have a dark side if I am to be whole'?
meta.ogDescription: The popular one-liner is a trimmed version of a real Jung sentence from "Problems of Modern Psychotherapy." Wikiquote carries the short form with no citation.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1875–1961 · Swiss psychiatrist, founder of analytical psychology
answer.sourceLine: Jung wrote something very close to this: a sentence documented in The Practice of Psychotherapy (Collected Works vol. 16, p. 59) reads “How can I be substantial without casting a shadow? I must have a dark side too if I am to be whole.” The popular one-liner is that sentence trimmed and lightly reordered — and we could not confirm the circulating wording against a primary text. Wikiquote lists the short form under “Attributed,” with no citation ↗.

source.heading: Where the real sentence lives

docMeta.dd: The Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 16: The Practice of Psychotherapy, 2nd ed. (Princeton University Press, 1966), pp. 53–75

source.excerpt: How can I be substantial without casting a shadow? I must have a dark side too if I am to be whole…
trail: Wikiquote ↗ places the popular short form in its “Attributed” list — no work, no page, no date. That is the honest starting point: the line as shared is unsourced.
A sourced Jungian anthology prints the full sentence and cites it to CW 16, p. 59 ↗, together with the clause that follows about remembering you are a human being like any other.

The International Association for Analytical Psychology’s abstracts for CW 16 ↗ place “Problems of Modern Psychotherapy” at pp. 53–75 of the 1966 Princeton edition — the page cited above falls inside that essay.

The same essay had appeared in English three decades earlier in Modern Man in Search of a Soul (1933) ↗, translated by Cary F. Baynes with W. S. Dell — which is why two English wordings compete online.
source.excerptNote: The 1933 Dell & Baynes translation of the same passage instead reads “How can I be substantial if I fail to cast a shadow?”

source.rightsNote: Both documented English sources are modern and protected: Modern Man in Search of a Soul was first published in 1933 and the Collected Works vol. 16 translation in 1966, so neither is in the US public domain. The circulating short form cannot be tied to any pre-1931 publication, so treat this line as in-copyright and quote it briefly with attribution.

author.name: Carl Jung
author.heading: About Carl Jung
author.metaLine: 1875–1961 · Swiss psychiatrist & founder of analytical psychology
author.bio: Carl Gustav Jung was a Swiss psychiatrist and psychotherapist who founded analytical psychology, breaking with Freud in the 1910s to pursue his own account of the unconscious. He gave psychology the vocabulary of the shadow, the anima, introversion and extraversion, and the collective unconscious. His writings on the shadow — the disowned part of the self — are the reason lines like this one circulate under his name, sometimes accurately and sometimes not.

cite.sourceCitation: C. G. Jung, “Problems of Modern Psychotherapy,” in The Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 16, The Practice of Psychotherapy, 2nd ed. (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1966), pp. 53–75; the passage at p. 59. The essay’s earlier English rendering by W. S. Dell and Cary F. Baynes appears in Modern Man in Search of a Soul (London: Kegan Paul, 1933), pp. 34–36. The exact popular wording — “I must also have a dark side if I am to be whole” — is not confirmed in either.

misattribution.heading: Right author, rewritten sentence
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is claiming this line — the problem is not who but what. The wording that spread is not the wording either English translation of Jung actually prints.

items.why: “I must also have a dark side if I am to be whole” moves “also” forward and drops “too”; the sourced passage reads “I must have a dark side too if I am to be whole” ↗.

The sentence is the answer to a question Jung asks immediately before it — “How can I be substantial if I fail to cast a shadow?” in the 1933 translation ↗ — which quote sites almost always strip away.
Goodreads carries the line under Carl Jung with no book or page at all ↗, and notes that its quotes are user-added and unverified.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is authentically Jung’s and a nearly identical sentence is documented in “Problems of Modern Psychotherapy,” CW 16 ↗ — but the exact line you have seen shared is a paraphrase of it, not a quotation from it.

context.heading: Why the missing half matters
lead: The line people share is only the second half of a two-part thought. In the documented passage Jung first asks a question — how can a person be substantial, have weight and reality, without casting a shadow? — and only then draws the conclusion about needing a dark side. Detached from the question, the sentence reads like a licence for one’s worst impulses. In place, it is an argument about honesty: what is inferior in you is still yours, and pretending otherwise makes you less real, not more.

The passage sits in an essay on the practice of psychotherapy, not in a book of aphorisms. Jung is describing what happens in the consulting room when a patient stops performing virtue — and the sentence that follows the famous one, in the Collected Works wording, is about recognising that you are a human being like any other.
detailsBody: Two English wordings are in circulation because two translations exist. The version in Modern Man in Search of a Soul (1933), translated by W. S. Dell and Cary F. Baynes, runs “How can I be substantial if I fail to cast a shadow?” The later Collected Works text uses “How can I be substantial without casting a shadow?” Neither matches the internet’s short form, which is why quote sites carry it uncited.
